For neither had the virgins robbed other men's goods, but they had not given their own; neither had he that buried the one talent embezzled, but he had not doubled; neither are they that overlooked the hungry punished, because they seized the possessions of others, but because they did not lay out their own, like as also this servant.

Let us hearken, as many as please the belly, as many as lay out on costly banquets the riches that pertain not at all to us, but belong to the needy. For do not, because out of great love to man thou art commanded to give as of thine, therefore suppose these things to be indeed thine own. He lent them to thee, that thou mightest be able to approve thyself. Do not then suppose them to be thine, when giving Him His own. For neither, if thou hadst lent to any one, that he might go and be able to find means of gain, wouldest thou say the money was his. To thee then also hath God given, that thou mightest traffic for Heaven. Make not then the exceeding greatness of His love to man a cause of ingratitude.

Though the Lord had given above a general exhortation to all in common to unwearied vigilance, yet He adds a special charge to the rulers of the people, that is, the Bishops, of watchfulness in looking for His coming. Such He calls a faithful servant, and wise master of the household, careful for the needs and interests of the people entrusted to Him.
Nor yet does it imply the impossibility of attaining perfect virtue, but only the difficulty.

Or, he that makes progress in the faith, though he is not yet perfect in it, is ordinarily called faithful, and he who has natural quickness of intellect is called prudent. And whoever observes will find many faithful, and zealous in their belief, but not at the same time prudent; for God hath chosen the foolish things of the world. (1 Cor. 1:27.) Others again he will see who are quick and prudent but of weak faith; for the union of faith and prudence in the same man is most rare. To give food in due season calls for prudence in a man; not to take away the food of the needy requires faithfulness. And this the literal sense obliges us to, that we be faithful in dispersing the revenues of the Church, that we devour not that which belongs to the widows, that we remember the poor, and that we do not take occasion from what is written, The Lord hath ordained, that they which preach the Gospel should live of the Gospel, (1 Cor. 9:14.) to seek more than plain food and necessary clothing, or to keep more for ourselves than we give to those who suffer want. And that we be prudent, to understand the cases of them that are in need, whence they come to be so, what has been the education and what are the necessities of each. It needs much prudence to distribute fairly the revenues of the Church. Also let the servant be faithful and prudent, that he lavish not the intellectual and spiritual food upon those whom he ought not, but dispense according as each has need; to one is more behoveful that word which shall edify his behaviour, and guide his practice, than that which sheds a ray of science; but to others who can pierce more deeply let him not fail to expound the deeper things, lest if he set before them common things only, he be despised by such as have naturally keener understandings, or have been sharpened by the discipline of worldly learning.

Who then is the faithful and prudent servant, whom his lord has set over his household, to give them food in due season?

That this parable pertains to the apostles and the other bishops and teachers is clear, especially from the fact that in Luke Peter asks, saying: "Do you speak this parable to us, or also to all?" Yet, although there are many stewards, it is difficult to find one who is both faithful and prudent. For this reason the Apostle says: "Let a man so account of us as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Here now it is required among stewards that a man be found faithful." But he sins against God, whatever bishop ministers not as a servant to fellow-servants but as a lord, and often even as a bitter lord domineering by force — set up like the Egyptians who afflicted the life of the sons of Israel with violence. Therefore they ought to be mindful of the words of Christ, who says: "You call me master and lord, and you say well; for so I am. If then I have washed your feet, you too ought to wash one another's feet; for I have given you an example, that as I have done, so you also should do." And that other saying: "The princes of the Gentiles domineer over them, and their greater ones exercise power over them. But among you it shall not be so; but whoever wishes to be first among you, shall be last; even as the Son of Man came not to be ministered to, but to minister, and to give his life a redemption for many." One ought also to hear Paul saying: "Whereas we might be a burden as apostles of Christ, we became little ones in your midst, just as if a nurse were to cherish her own children; so, in our longing, we desire to share with you not only the Gospel, but also our own souls"; and one ought not to strike fellow-servants, but to "rebuke the unruly, comfort the fainthearted, uphold the weak, and be patient toward all," since "the servant of God ought not to quarrel but to be gentle toward all, teaching with modesty those who resist." And as one himself withdrawing from the evil enticement of fellow-servants, Paul blames those who were not such, who were indeed subject to the proud but despised the gentle, speaking in this manner: "You endure it if any man reduces you to servitude, if any devours, if any takes, if any exalts himself, if any strikes you in the face, as though we had been weak."

But consider in these words how he reproves those who reduce to servitude and strike in the face — because of which they domineer the more bitterly — saying that he himself abstains from these things; not because he was too weak to do them, but that he might do the very things he teaches. And he teaches to teach "with modesty" "those who resist." For this reason too, defining what sort bishops ought to be, he speaks thus: "not quarrelsome, not strikers, but gentle, well-ordered," and whatever qualities are found among faithful and wise servants and stewards, whom "the lord has set over his household," as Luke says. And from these things it may be recognized that not only those who are faithful and wise does the lord set over his household, but also the wicked servants who say ever in their hearts: "My lord delays his coming"; and therefore they strike their fellow-servants, eat and drink with the drunken or with drunkards, and become inebriated. If, then, at any time those who preside over the churches of Christ suppose themselves to be at a great height, because "the lord has set them over his household," let them recognize that it is not this that saves them, that they were set by the lord over his household, but rather that they should give food in due season, and that they should abstain from strikings and from carousings and drinkings with drunkards. But if they do not abstain from such things, and are haughty because the lord has set them over his household, let them know that their lord will come in a day on which they do not look and at an hour which they do not know, and will divide them, and will set their portion with the hypocrites and the unfaithful; and when they have been set among the hypocrites and the unfaithful, it will profit them nothing that they were set by the lord over his household.

But that we may fear that which he says, he will divide him, it is fitting to recall the things said by Daniel against the wicked elders, namely that "the angel of God, having a sword, will cut you in two"; and in cutting, he divides.

We have ventured to use in this place the example from Daniel, not being ignorant that it is not found in the Hebrew, but because it is held in the churches; to inquire about such a matter belongs to another time.

But attend also to this, that he says faithful servant and prudent, hearing the word kindly and acquiescing in the will of Christ, who speaks these things, and of Matthew, who writes them down. Diligently, therefore, must we hear about the faithful and prudent servant: he who advances in faith, or (if he is not yet perfect in it) he who commonly is himself also called faithful, and he who has a natural quickness of mind and is called prudent. For the steward of iniquity too "acted prudently," not indeed acting according to prudence as one of the virtues, but because he was quick in wit. And "the sons of this age are more prudent than the sons of light in their generation," not because they are prudent according to prudence as one of the virtues, or because the sons of light are inferior to them in any other respect in wisdom, except that in worldly wisdom or in natural sharpness of mind they are inferior; for the divine word knows also that prudence is one of the virtues, as it teaches in Proverbs, saying: Say that wisdom is your sister, and make prudence known to you, that it may guard you from the strange woman.

But now we ought to hear in a general sense what he says: who is the faithful and prudent servant, as though some indeed are faithful according to faith as commonly understood, but are not prudent nor quick in wit; and again others are indeed quick and, in the sense here signified, prudent, but not altogether faithful as well. But if one considers the multitude of those wishing to be Christians, he will find indeed many faithful and exercising zeal for the faith, but not also prudent, so that the sons of this age are more prudent than they in their generation, knowing that God has chosen the foolish things of the world, that he may confound the wise. And again he will see others, who are thought to have believed, who are indeed quick and wise, but of small faith and, if not unfaithful, yet less faithful than the foolish things of the world which God has chosen. But that faithful and prudent should meet together in one man, so that according to both he gives his fellow-servants food in due season, is very rare indeed. For to give food in due season to the needy, one has need of prudence; but that one should not withhold food in due season from the needy, there is need of faith.

Nor is it inopportune to give warning on account of the sins which, in men who seem to believe in Christ and in the stewards of the churches, are for the most part wont to occur, since even according to the simple sense many of us have need to be faithful and likewise prudent for dispensing the revenues of the church: faithful indeed, that we may not devour what belongs to widows and that we may be mindful of the poor, and, taking occasion from that which is written: the Lord has ordained for those who preach the Gospel to live by the Gospel, that we may not seek more than simple food and necessary clothing, that we may not keep back for ourselves more than we give to the hungry and thirsty and naked brethren and to those who suffer need amid worldly cares; prudent, moreover, that we may minister to each one according to each one's worthiness, remembering what has been said: "Blessed is he who has understanding concerning the needy and poor." For we ought not to give from the church's goods simply, so that we observe this one thing only, that we not devour what belongs to the poor or commit theft from it, but that we prudently understand the circumstances of the needy on account of which they are needy, and the standing of each — how he was brought up, how much he has need of, or for what cause he is in want. Therefore one must not act in the same way toward those who from infancy have been brought up hardly and strictly, and toward those who have been nourished lavishly and delicately and afterward have fallen. Nor are the same things to be ministered to men and to women, or to the very old and to the young, or indeed to the young but feeble (because of which they cannot procure food for themselves) and to those who can in part relieve themselves. It must also be inquired whether they have many children, not being negligent but doing all things and yet not sufficiently providing for themselves. And, that we may not say more, there is need of much wisdom for one who wishes to dispense well the revenues of the church, so that in these matters too, being found a faithful and prudent steward, he may be made blessed.

But perhaps also, on account of the multitude of Christians who are not held in sufficient regard concerning the searching of the word and yet are such as have been raised to leadership, we have all the more need to hear: who is the faithful and prudent servant whom the lord has set over his household, to give them food in due season? — that they may not pour out the rational and spiritual food upon fellow-servants of whatever sort indiscriminately and upon those to whom they ought not, wishing to show themselves prudent, when rather those have more need of the word that builds up their morals and orders their life, than of that which leads forward to wisdom and illuminates with the light of knowledge those whose mind can bear the splendor of such a light; or that they may not be reluctant to expound the higher things to those who are able to hear more keenly, lest by expounding cheap things they be despised by the more clever, who are naturally clever or perhaps are held to be sharp through the exercise of worldly wisdom. It is difficult, therefore, for both to be in one man, that he be both prudent and faithful, yet not impossible; for he does not pronounce blessed one who cannot exist, when he says: Blessed is that servant, whom his lord, when he comes, shall find so doing. Amen I say to you, that he will set him over all his goods.
That is, obedient to his Lord's command, by the seasonableness of his teaching dispensing the word of life to a household which is to be nourished for the food of eternity.

Blessed is that servant, whom his lord, when he comes, shall find so doing. A great promise is proclaimed to faithful and prudent stewards, and it accords with those to whom he says: "be thou having authority over five cities", or: "be thou having authority over ten cities". For to be set over all the goods of the head of the household — what else does this make plain but that they are "heirs of God and joint-heirs with Christ" and reign together with Christ, to whom the Father has handed over all his own things, as he himself says: "all power has been given to me in heaven and on earth"? And (in the manner of the son of a good father) being set over all the substance of the father, he shares this same dignity and glory with his faithful and prudent stewards, so that they too may be over every creature and power, so that they may be with Christ. And observe his interpretation of what he says: amen I say to you, that he will set him over all his goods. Understand for me (taking it as if by way of example) some king who has an entire kingdom under himself, with whom are many nations and cities and diverse places. Let him, then, divide among his satraps and the other princes, who have done something notably well, the fullness of his kingdom; and let him indeed set all of them over his whole kingdom, yet not each one over all things — but each one of them over some part of his kingdom: for instance, one indeed over ten cities, another over five. And thus they will all be over all the goods, while he alone holds all things, being, as it were, the sole king of all. And such is what he says: he will set him over all his goods.

But just as we have heard concerning the blessedness to be given to the faithful and prudent servants, so let us also hear concerning the torments of the wicked servants. For the wicked servant speaks in his heart, preferring present pleasure to the goods to come, and, despising his lord, he says: my lord delays to come; but he says this lying, wishing to eat and drink with the drunkards. And he is always dreaming that after a long time his lord will come; and, as though his lord were delaying, he strikes the fellow servants who endure it, and reduces them to servitude, and beats them in the face; and, striking them, he eats and drinks with the drunkards, under the pretext of ecclesiastical service, and he does not receive the hungry but feasts with the drunkards. And there are many of this kind to whom the ecclesiastical charge has been committed, upon whom the lord will come, bringing about their consummation on the day on which they do not know and at the hour at which they do not expect, and he will divide them — those who have not feared him who "is able to destroy soul and body in hell".

And he will divide him, when "his spirit indeed returns to God who gave it", but his soul together with its body goes "into hell".

The just man, however, is not divided, but his soul goes with his spirit to the heavenly kingdoms; on account of which it is written: "bless the Lord, ye spirits and souls of the just". But of those who are divided and lay down the spirit that returns to him who had given it, and thereafter do not have in themselves any part which was from God, there is left to them their part which was their own, that is, the soul, which together with its body will be punished by the lord when he comes, with the hypocrites and the "unfaithful" in torments.

See, therefore, the difference among the servants whom the lord has set over his household, since certain ones indeed, as faithful and prudent stewards who gave food to their fellow servants in due time, are set over all the goods of the head of the household; but those who have done things contrary to these, apart from the fact that they have fallen from so great a glory, will moreover be divided, and their part will be placed with the hypocrites and the "unfaithful". There will be weeping for those who wickedly laughed in this world, as the Scripture says: "woe to you who now laugh, for you shall weep and mourn". And consequently, on account of the rest and the relaxation in which they took their rest and were relaxed, there will reasonably be for them a gnashing of teeth: which perhaps signifies this, that those who are punished, thinking that there will be an end of their pain and on this account wishing to endure it manfully, being driven by unendurable torments, gnash with their teeth — with those teeth, namely, with which they ate the bitterness of malice, and therefore they suffer a fitting gnashing of teeth.

Though the Lord had given above a general exhortation to all in common to unwearied vigilance, yet He adds a special charge to the rulers of the people, that is, the Bishops, of watchfulness in looking for His coming. Such He calls a faithful servant, and wise master of the household, careful for the needs and interests of the people entrusted to Him. That is, obedient to his Lord's command, by the seasonableness of his teaching dispensing the word of life to a household which is to be nourished for the food of eternity.
Or, shall set him over all his goods, that is, shall place him in the glory of God, because beyond this is nothing better.

It should be observed, that as there is great difference of desert between good preachers and good hearers, so is there great difference between their rewards. The good hearers, if He finds them watching He will make to sit down to meat, as Luke speaks; but the good preachers He will set over all His goods.

That he may reign with Christ, to whom the Father has committed all that is His. And as the son of a good father set over all that is his, He shall communicate of His dignity and glory to His faithful and wise stewards, that they also may be above the whole creation.

(Ep. 199. 1.) The temper of this servant is shown in his behaviour, which is thus expressed by his good Master; his tyranny, and shall begin to beat his fellow servants, his sensuality, and to eat and drink with the drunken. So that when he said, My Lord delayeth His coming, he is not to be supposed to speak from desire to see the Lord, such as was that of him who said, My soul is athirst for the living God; when shall I come? (Ps. 42:2.) This shows that he was grieved at the delay, seeing that what was hastening towards him seemed to his longing desires to be coming slowly.

And every Bishop, who ministers not as a fellow servant, but rules by might as a master, and often an harsh one, sins against God; also if he does not cherish the needy, but feasts with the drunken, and is continually slumbering because his Lord cometh not till after long time.

(Ep. 199 in fin.) Putting aside this wicked servant, who, there is no doubt, hates his Master's coming, let us set before our eyes these good servants, who anxiously expect their Lord's coming. One looks for His coming sooner, another later, the third confesses his ignorance of the matter. Let us see which is most agreeable to the Gospel. One says, Let us watch and pray, because the Lord will quickly come; another, Let us watch and pray, because this life is short and uncertain, though the Lord's coming may be distant; and the third, Let us watch, because this life is short and uncertain, and we know not the time when the Lord will come. What else does this man say than what we hear the Gospel say, Watch, because ye know not the hour in which the Lord shall come? All indeed, through longing for the kingdom, desire that that should be true which the first thinks, and if it should so come to pass, the second and third would rejoice with him; but if it should not come to pass, it were to be feared that the belief of its supporters might be shaken by the delay, and they might begin to think that the Lord's coming shall be, not remote, but never. He who believes with the second that the Lord's coming is distant will not be shaken in faith, but will receive an unlooked for joy. He who confesses his ignorance which of these is true, wishes for the one, is resigned to the other, but errs in neither, because he neither affirms or denies either.
The Lord of that servant shall come in a day when he looketh not for Him, is to rouse the stewards to watchfulness and carefulness.

He shall cut him in sunder, is not to be understood of execution by the sword, but that he shall sever him from the company of the saints.

And shall appoint him his portion with the hypocrites, with those, namely, that were in the field, and grinding at the mill, and were nevertheless left. For as we often say that the hypocrite is one who is one thing, and passes himself for another; so in the field and at the mill he seemed to be doing the same as others, but the event proved that his purpose was different.

Or, He shall cut him in sunder, when his spirit, that is, his spiritual gift, shall return to God who gave it; but his soul shall go with his body into hell. But the righteous man is not cut in sunder, but his soul, with his spirit, that is, with his gift, spiritual enters into the kingdom of heaven. They that are cut in sunder have in the in thenceforth no part of that spiritual gift which was from God, but there remains to them that part which was their own, that is, their soul, which shall be punished with their body.

Or, there shall be weeping for such as have laughed amiss in this world, gnashing of teeth for those who have enjoyed an irrational peace. For being unwilling to suffer bodily pain, now the torture forces their teeth to chatter, with which they have eaten the bitterness of wickedness. From this we may learn that the Lord sets over His household not the faithful and wise only, but the wicked also; and that it will not save them to have been set over His household, but only if they have given them their food in due season, and have abstained from beating and drunkenness.
